solutions.check: 31 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: (& 26dn.) Slush fund ultimately takes the piss out of the police?

indicators.note: What comes ultimately comes last of all, so only the final letter of the word beside it is taken.

blocks.note: slush underfoot is soft sloppy stuff, and goo is the word for anything that sticky
the last letter of the word, which is all the instruction beside it wants
to guy a person is to hold them up to ridicule

explanation.surface: Money kept off the books making a mockery of the force.
explanation.walkthrough: To guy someone is to mock them, the verb behind Guy Fawkes and the effigy burnt in his name. The question mark concedes that the police are only one example of the side in the white hats.
explanation.definitionFit: The good guys are whichever side is supposed to be on the side of right, so the police are named as an instance of them rather than by synonym.

clue.text: Minister left with rising anger when pressed by Conservatives

indicators.note: In a down entry the letters climb the column, so the word beside this one is written from the bottom up.
Someone pressed by a crowd has it closing on either side, so the letters so far go between the pair that follows.

blocks.note: C is the party's letter on a ballot paper, and more than one Conservative gives two of them, one for each side
the usual single letter for left, as in a stage direction
ire is anger in its oldest form; those three letters are then read up the column

explanation.surface: A government minister losing his temper under pressure from Tory MPs.
explanation.walkthrough: Minister sits in a sentence about parties and pressure, so it reads as a politician; the church sense is what the grid wants. The plural Conservatives is the only sign that two letters are wanted rather than one.
explanation.definitionFit: A cleric is a man in holy orders, and minister is what a congregation calls the man who leads its worship.

clue.text: (& 28dn.)Loopy thing awfully keen to nick fellow in balls

indicators.note: Something done awfully is done badly, and letters handled badly do not stay in the order they were given.
To nick a thing is to take it, so the shuffled letters take the next piece inside them.
What is in something sits within it, so everything before goes inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: rot is talk not worth listening to, which is what balls means in this sense; the word parts after its first letter
four letters to be re-set, and they open in the middle to take what is nicked
F is the fellow of a learned society, as in FRS

explanation.surface: A thief so eager that he goes for a man's privates.
explanation.walkthrough: Loopy sounds like mad and here means made of loops, which is the whole joke of the definition. Balls is the vulgar noun in the picture and the mild one in the wordplay, where it is only nonsense talk.
explanation.definitionFit: A reef knot is tied from two loops pulled against each other, so loopy thing names what it is made of rather than what it does.

clue.text: Despairing American-backed island police force needs a lift initially

indicators.note: Something backed has been turned to face the other way, so the letters before it are written in reverse.
A word taken initially gives up its opening letter and nothing else.

blocks.note: the United States shortened to its two letters, which are then read the other way about
I is the map-maker's short form for island
the Criminal Investigation Department is the plain-clothes detective branch of a British police force
the article taken as it stands
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: An island's detectives, propped up by Washington and badly in need of a boost.
explanation.walkthrough: CID is the detective branch every British force has, always initialled and never spelled out. 'Needs a lift' reads as wanting cheering up, which is the mood the definition names, so the wordplay hides inside the sentence's own complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone suicidal has given up on living altogether, which is despairing carried to its end.

clue.text: Isle's broadcaster on ecstasy

blocks.note: Sky is the satellite company that carries much of British television
E is what the drug is called on the street

explanation.surface: A television company high on a dance drug.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry one thing on another sits above it, which is where the broadcaster goes. Skye is the largest of the Inner Hebrides, off the west coast of Scotland and reached now by bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Skye is one particular island, so isle defines it by its kind rather than by a synonym.

clue.text: It facilitates motion without shifting

blocks.note: reads as a machine that helps things travel, and means the other motion, the one a doctor asks a patient about
nobody has to cross the room to reach it, which is the point of keeping one beside the bed

explanation.surface: A device that gets things moving while never moving itself.
explanation.walkthrough: Motion is the word with two lives: travel in the sentence, and the bowel's business in the answer. A commode is the chair with a chamber pot under its seat, and no fragment of the clue hands over a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A commode is a bedside chair with a pot beneath the lid, so anyone who cannot walk to the bathroom has the motion it exists for without going anywhere.

clue.text: Small sculptor's Burn with Suppressed Lust

blocks.note: S is the size on a clothing label
a sculptor working in clay moulds it, so the man himself is a moulder

explanation.surface: A miniature sculptor burning with a desire he is keeping to himself.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals on Burn, Suppressed and Lust are decoration — Cyclops sets the phrase up as a title, and not a letter comes of them. Moulder is simply one who moulds, a word the dictionary keeps for the sculptor's sake.
explanation.definitionFit: To smoulder is to burn without flame, and of a person it means exactly that desire held down and showing anyway.

clue.text: Get tight

blocks.note: the sense used of a contract or a seat on a plane: to succeed in obtaining the thing
of a knot or a lid, fastened so firmly that nothing will work it loose

explanation.surface: An instruction to go out and get drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: Tight is British for drunk, which is the whole of the picture and none of the meaning. Two words, two senses, and nothing joining them but the space between.
explanation.definitionFit: To secure a contract is to get it, and a lid screwed down so that nothing shifts is tight in the fastening sense.

clue.text: Stupid intrusive time announcer

blocks.note: the informal adjective for somebody soft in the head
the bird that pushes its egg into another bird's nest, and the carved one that pops out of a clock on the hour

explanation.surface: A halfwit who keeps butting in to tell everyone what the time is.
explanation.walkthrough: Cuckoo for crazy comes from the bird's flat two-note call. The second definition wants bird and clock at once: the intruder lays in other birds' nests, the wooden one springs out on the hour.
explanation.definitionFit: Cuckoo is the informal word for stupid, and the cuckoo both forces its egg into a nest not its own and calls the hours out of a clock.

clue.text: Balls squeezed by Bentley? Getting wood!

indicators.note: What is squeezed by a thing is pressed inside it, so the letters before go within the word that follows.

blocks.note: a Bentley is a make of car, and the word parts after its first letter
the capital letter points at Ed Balls, Labour's shadow chancellor until he lost his seat in 2015

explanation.surface: Something painful happening to a man's balls in a Bentley, with an erection as the result.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting wood' is the clue's crude joke and the timber is what the grid wants, which is the only sense in which the exclamation mark is honest. Surnames that are also common nouns are Cyclops's stock trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Cedar is the fragrant reddish timber used for chests and cigar boxes, so wood names the material the tree gives.

clue.text: Farce: came explosively (good for the skin?)

definitions.note: The definition says what the answer is for instead of naming it, so an adjective phrase stands where a noun would; the question mark inside the bracket admits as much.

indicators.note: Something that goes off explosively is blown apart, and the letters land in none of their old places.

blocks.note: five letters to be re-set
four more letters joining the shuffle

explanation.surface: A ridiculous business that ended with somebody coming explosively.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Came explosively' is the clue's dirty joke and the plainest anagram instruction in the puzzle at the same time. The colon after the first word is the only join, and it says nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Face-cream is rubbed into the skin to keep it soft, so the bracket names what the stuff is for rather than what it is.

clue.text: No life in this rogue state

definitions.note: The definition describes the answer — a body with nothing left alive in it — instead of naming it, so a whole phrase stands where a noun would.

blocks.note: a cad is a rogue of the ungentlemanly sort, the man who lets a lady down
to aver something is to state it flatly, the word a lawyer uses

explanation.surface: A country run by scoundrels where nothing survives.
explanation.walkthrough: Rogue state is one phrase in the sentence and two separate words in the wordplay, which is the whole of the difficulty here. Neither half is a noun once the phrase is broken up.
explanation.definitionFit: A cadaver is a corpse, the word anatomists and pathologists use, so the phrase describes the one thing that tells it from a body.

clue.text: Moved to declare "bollocks"?

indicators.note: To bollocks a job up is to make a mess of it, and letters in a mess do not keep the order they came in.

blocks.note: two letters taken as they stand and thrown into the shuffle
seven more letters to be re-set

explanation.surface: Somebody stirred enough by what they have heard to call it rubbish out loud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moved to' reads as prompted, the way anyone is moved to speak, and the definition wants the other sense, shifted somewhere else. The quotation marks dress the last word as an outburst when it is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: To relocate is to move house or move premises, so moved is the same verb in the same tense.

clue.text: see 15ac.
Bent, did a granddad dance?

blocks.note: out of true, whether it is a length of wire or a man's morals
the dance craze of 1962, so anybody old enough to be a grandfather now was doing it then

explanation.surface: A question about whether a stooping old man got up and danced.
explanation.walkthrough: The Twist swept Britain in 1962, which makes the granddad in the sentence exactly the generation that did it. Bent carries the crooked sense as well as the shape, and either reading lands on the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: Twisted is bent out of true, crooked in both the physical and the criminal sense, and anyone who danced the Twist twisted.

clue.text: (&13dn.) Minister: crazy lady, mad with MI5

indicators.note: A crazy arrangement is one nobody would have chosen, so the letters that follow are re-set in a new order.

blocks.note: four letters to be re-set
three more letters joining the shuffle, the word standing for itself rather than instructing
the Security Service's initials with its number written as the Roman five

explanation.surface: A minister, a deranged woman and the Security Service tangled up in one sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: MI5 has to be read as two letters and a numeral, V being the Roman five, which is the neatest piece of fodder in the puzzle. David Lammy was Deputy Prime Minister and Justice Secretary when this puzzle ran.
explanation.definitionFit: David Lammy is the Labour MP who sat in the Cabinet, so minister names the office and the answer is the man holding it.

clue.text: Utter failing to crush ball

indicators.note: To crush a thing is to squeeze it, and what is squeezed ends up inside, so the letter named goes within the word before it.

blocks.note: a vice is a moral failing, and the word parts after its first letter
a ball is round, and the round letter is O

explanation.surface: Somebody not quite managing to crush a ball.
explanation.walkthrough: Vice is the moral failing and also the workshop tool that does the crushing, which is the joke sitting under the surface. Utter is the verb, to say a thing aloud, not the adjective meaning complete.
explanation.definitionFit: To voice an objection is to say it aloud, which is what utter means when it is a verb.

clue.text: Intriguer Henry, caught by Camilla, "I've screwed around"

indicators.note: Somebody caught by another is held inside, so the single letter goes in among the letters around it.
A thing screwed around has been twisted out of position, so the letters end up in none of their old places.

blocks.note: seven letters to be re-set, opening to take what is caught inside
three more letters joining the shuffle, the apostrophe dropped
H is the henry, the unit of inductance named after the physicist

explanation.surface: A schemer called Henry caught by Camilla, admitting he has slept around.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry is the electrical unit, not the king: inductance is measured in henries and written H. Niccolò Machiavelli advised the rulers of Florence in The Prince, and his name has meant a political schemer ever since.
explanation.definitionFit: Machiavelli's own name became the word for a political schemer, so intriguer defines the man by what he has come to stand for.

clue.text: Officers must cover genital area by end of the Fall

indicators.note: To cover a thing is to lie over it on both sides.
The end of a word is its last letter, and that letter is all that is taken.

blocks.note: Col is the army's short form for colonel and more than one adds the S; the letters part after the third
the lap is the front of the body between waist and knees when a person is sitting down
the last letter of the definite article, which is a word of the clue like any other

explanation.surface: Officers told to keep their private parts covered until autumn is over.
explanation.walkthrough: Fall is the American word for autumn in the sentence and the plain English noun in the definition. The piece that finishes the answer comes out of 'the', which solvers read past without counting it as fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A collapse is what a building or a market does when it falls in on itself, so fall is the same noun in plainer clothes.

clue.text: Deflated by peer, this baron takes steps

definitions.note: The definition says what is done to the answer instead of naming it, and it only works if peer is heard as one who pees.

blocks.note: B is the short form for baron in lists of the peerage
a set of steps is a ladder, rung by rung

explanation.surface: A baron put down by a fellow member of the Lords and doing something about it.
explanation.walkthrough: Peer is a fellow member of the Lords in the sentence and one who pees in the joke, and the joke is what does the deflating. 'Takes steps' reads as taking action, so the second half of the wordplay hides in an idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: A bladder is the bag that holds urine, and it goes down as it empties, so one who pees is what flattens it.

clue.text: Cutting end off diplomat's tie

indicators.note: Cutting the end off a word takes its last letter away and leaves everything before it untouched.

blocks.note: the French title of the junior specialist posted to an embassy, the military one or the cultural one, kept in English without its accent

explanation.surface: Snipping the end off a diplomat's necktie.
explanation.walkthrough: Tie is the verb here, not the thing round the diplomat's neck, and that swap is the trap the surface sets. The apostrophe-s is the setter's join rather than anything the wordplay needs.
explanation.definitionFit: To attach one thing to another is to tie it on, so the two verbs swap without changing the sentence.

clue.text: Kate, say, changed political sides initially? True

indicators.note: When a thing is changed, one piece comes out and another goes in its place, and here the pieces are single letters.
Taken initially means taken at the front, so each word named gives up its opening letter alone.

blocks.note: Kate, the Princess of Wales, is one of them, and 'say' marks her as an example rather than a synonym
Right and Left are the two sides in politics, so their opening letters are R and L, and the L comes in for the R

explanation.surface: A royal quietly switching which party she backs.
explanation.walkthrough: Political sides are Right and Left before they are parties, and only the initials of those two words matter. The question mark covers the switch being described rather than spelled out.
explanation.definitionFit: A loyal friend is a true friend — true in the older sense of staying faithful, not of being correct.

clue.text: Raging: "Endless shit, endless twaddle, little entertainment!"

indicators.note: A word made endless has had its end taken off, so its final letter never appears.
The same instruction a second time: the word beside it loses its last letter.
A little of a word is a shortened form of it, here the three letters the word is habitually cut down to.

blocks.note: a turd is a piece of excrement, docked of its last letter
bull is talk that means nothing, with its last letter gone
ent is the printed short form, the one student unions put on their posters

explanation.surface: A viewer's furious verdict: nothing on but rubbish and nothing worth watching.
explanation.walkthrough: Three complaints in quotation marks read as one loss of temper and work as three separate words to be cut short. The colon and the quotes carry no instruction at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A turbulent crowd or a turbulent priest is one raging out of control, so the adjective and raging describe the same behaviour.

clue.text: Excited fellow feeling arrogant

blocks.note: somebody excited is up, in high spirits
fellow feeling is what you have for a person whose trouble you can imagine having yourself

explanation.surface: A man worked up and sorry for somebody at the same time.
explanation.walkthrough: Fellow feeling is one phrase, not a fellow and a feeling, and that is where the join hides. Uppity was what was said of people who would not keep to the place others had chosen for them.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody uppity gives themselves airs above their station, which is arrogance described from below.

clue.text: Ruthless competition when boxer put away another boxer?

blocks.note: a boxer is a breed, short-coated and square-jawed
a man who puts away three helpings has eaten them
the same breed a second time

explanation.surface: One prizefighter finishing another off in the ring.
explanation.walkthrough: Boxer is the prizefighter in the sentence and the breed in the wordplay, and the clue needs it both ways in the same breath. The question mark admits how literal-minded the picture is.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog eat dog trade is one where everybody preys on everybody else, which is competition with no rules left in it.

clue.text: Quite ready for a romp?

blocks.note: the sense a person means by saying they are up for it, willing to have a go at whatever is being suggested
a boisterous bit of fun, the sort children have in a field

explanation.surface: Asking whether somebody fancies a bit of fun.
explanation.walkthrough: The four words read as a single phrase and split into two definitions at 'for', which is the whole of the trick. Romp is the racier noun on the surface and the innocent one underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody game is quite ready to join in whatever is proposed, and a romp is a game of the boisterous sort.

clue.text: see 1dn.
Crap UK karaoke hosts "genuine"

indicators.note: A host keeps the guest inside the house, so the letters sit unbroken within the words before the word itself.

blocks.note: the letters run on across both word breaks, in the order they are written

explanation.surface: A terrible British karaoke night putting on something authentic.
explanation.walkthrough: Pukka came into English from Hindi with the Raj, where it meant solid or properly built, and has stayed as the word for the real article. Hosts is the concealment instruction and reads as the compère of the evening.
explanation.definitionFit: Pukka means the real thing rather than an imitation, which is genuine in plainer English.

clue.text: see 3dn.
She's about to embrace 'new' Cyclops? "Get knotted!"

indicators.note: What is thrown about lands anywhere, so the letters beside the word do not keep the order they came in.
To embrace is to put both arms right round, so the letters just re-set open and take the next pieces inside.

blocks.note: three letters to be re-set, opening to take what is embraced
N is the single letter for new, as on a price label
Cyclops is the setter of this puzzle, so he writes himself in the way anybody refers to themselves

explanation.surface: A woman on the point of hugging a made-over setter.
explanation.walkthrough: Cyclops is the name at the top of the puzzle, and a setter naming himself means the two letters anyone uses for themselves. The quotation marks round 'new' mark a word wanted for its letter rather than its sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To enmesh somebody is to tangle them in a net, which is what get knotted asks for when it is meant literally rather than as an insult.

clue.text: Canine's organ too too hard initially

indicators.note: Taken initially means taken at the front, so each word named gives up its opening letter alone.

blocks.note: the organ of sight, three letters of it
the word written out as it stands
the opening letters of the two words, taken in the order they come

explanation.surface: A dog's member, stiff from the start and then some.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue says 'too' twice and uses the same word two ways, once whole and once for its first letter. A canine is the pointed tooth beside the incisors, which is also what a dog is.
explanation.definitionFit: The eyetooth is the canine of the upper jaw, the pointed one sitting under the eye, so canine names the tooth itself.
